chapter: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round (Circles, Class 9 Maths)
note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are
items.explanation: Every point of a circle is the same distance, the radius, from a fixed point called the centre.

options.why: That describes a pair of parallel lines, not a circle.
Collinear points lie on a straight line.

options.text: at different distances from a point
options.why: Varying distances would not produce a circle.

items.stem: The longest chord of a circle is called the
items.explanation: A chord through the centre is the diameter, and no chord can be longer.

options.why: The radius is half the diameter and is not a chord.
An arc is a curved part of the circle, not a straight segment.
A tangent touches the circle at one point and is not a chord.

items.stem: If the diameter of a circle is 14 cm, its radius is
items.explanation: The radius is half the diameter, so it is 7 cm.

options.why: This doubles the diameter instead of halving it.
This repeats the diameter rather than halving it.
This quarters the diameter instead of halving it.

items.stem: The angle in a semicircle is
items.explanation: An angle subtended by a diameter at any point of the circle is a right angle.

options.why: That is the angle of the straight diameter itself, not the angle at the circumference.
The angle is always a right angle, whatever the position of the point.
The angle is always a right angle, whatever the position of the point.

items.concept: Unique Circle Through Three Non-collinear Points
items.stem: The number of circles that can pass through three given non-collinear points is
items.explanation: Three non-collinear points determine exactly one circle, whose centre is the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors.

options.why: The perpendicular bisectors meet at a single point, giving one centre.
Infinitely many circles pass through two points, but three fix the circle.
Non-collinear points always admit a circle through them.

items.stem: A perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord
items.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre always bisects the chord.

options.why: The chord is divided into two equal parts, not three.
The perpendicular is a distance, unrelated in length to the chord.

options.text: meets the chord at its end
options.why: It meets the chord at its midpoint, not at an endpoint.

items.concept: Angle Subtended by an Arc at Centre
items.stem: An arc subtends an angle of 80 degrees at the centre. The angle it subtends at the remaining circumference is
items.explanation: The angle at the circumference is half the angle at the centre for the same arc.

options.why: This doubles the central angle instead of halving it.
The two angles are equal only if the theorem is misremembered.
This quarters the central angle instead of halving it.

items.stem: In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of a pair of opposite angles is
items.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, adding to 180 degrees.

options.why: Complementary angles are not what the cyclic property gives.
That is the sum of all four angles of any quadrilateral.
No standard circle theorem gives this sum.

items.concept: Equal Chords are Equidistant from Centre
items.stem: Two chords of a circle are equal in length. Their distances from the centre are
items.explanation: Equal chords are always equidistant from the centre, and the converse also holds.

options.text: in the ratio of the chords
options.why: The chords are equal, so any such ratio would be one anyway.
The theorem establishes a definite relation between them.
A distance of zero would make both chords diameters.

items.stem: The circumcentre of a triangle is found by intersecting the
items.explanation: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet at the point equidistant from all three vertices.

options.why: Those meet at the incentre, the centre of the inscribed circle.
Those meet at the centroid, the centre of mass.
Those meet at the orthocentre.

items.stem: Define the radius of a circle.
items.answer: The radius is the distance from the centre of the circle to any point on the circle, and it is the same for every such point.

items.stem: Why is every diameter a chord, but not every chord a diameter?
items.answer: A chord is any segment joining two points on the circle, and a diameter does exactly that, so it is a chord. A diameter must also pass through the centre, which most chords do not, so the reverse is not true.

items.stem: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
items.answer: Infinitely many. Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry, and there are infinitely many such lines.

items.stem: How many circles pass through two given distinct points?
items.answer: Infinitely many. The centre must lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, and every point of that line serves as a centre for some circle through both.

items.stem: Two angles are in the same segment of a circle. What can you say about them?
items.answer: They are equal. Angles subtended by the same arc at any two points on the remaining part of the circle are always equal, because each is half the same central angle.

items.concept: Line Joining Centre to Midpoint of Chord
items.stem: The line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord makes what angle with the chord?
items.answer: A right angle. This is the converse of the perpendicular bisector property: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is always perpendicular to it.

items.stem: What does it mean for four points to be concyclic, and how would you test it?
items.answer: Four points are concyclic if a single circle passes through all of them. A convenient test is to join them into a quadrilateral and check whether a pair of opposite angles adds to 180 degrees; if so, the points are concyclic.

items.stem: Is a parallelogram ever cyclic? Justify.
items.answer: Only if it is a rectangle. Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, and for it to be cyclic they must also add to 180 degrees, which forces each to be 90 degrees. So the only cyclic parallelograms are rectangles, including squares.

items.stem: Define the terms centre, radius, chord, diameter and arc for a circle.
items.answer: The centre is the fixed point from which every point of the circle is the same distance. The radius is that common distance, and also any segment from the centre to the circle. A chord is a segment joining any two points on the circle. A diameter is a chord that passes through the centre, and it is the longest chord, equal to twice the radius. An arc is a connected part of the circle itself, that is a piece of the curve rather than a straight segment; a diameter divides the circle into two equal arcs called semicircles.

items.stem: Describe the symmetries of a circle and explain why it has so many.
items.answer: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry, namely every line through its centre, and it also has rotational symmetry of every possible angle about its centre. The reason is that the circle is defined purely by distance from the centre. Reflecting in any line through the centre, or rotating by any angle about the centre, leaves every distance from the centre unchanged, so it maps the circle exactly onto itself. No other plane figure has this complete symmetry, which is why the circle is often taken as the most symmetrical shape.

items.stem: A chord of length 16 cm lies in a circle of radius 10 cm. Find its distance from the centre.
items.answer: Draw the perpendicular from the centre to the chord. It bisects the chord, so each half is 8 cm. This creates a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is the radius, 10 cm, one leg is half the chord, 8 cm, and the other leg is the required distance d. By the Pythagoras theorem, 10 squared equals 8 squared plus d squared, so 100 = 64 + d squared, giving d squared = 36 and d = 6 cm. The chord is therefore 6 cm from the centre.

items.stem: A chord is 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 13 cm. Find the length of the chord.
items.answer: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, forming a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 cm and one leg 5 cm. By the Pythagoras theorem the other leg is the square root of (169 - 25), which is the square root of 144, that is 12 cm. This is half the chord, so the full chord is 24 cm long. Note the general pattern: the closer a chord is to the centre, the longer it is, and the diameter is the chord at distance zero.

items.concept: Equal Chords Subtend Equal Angles at Centre
items.stem: Two chords of a circle are equal. Prove that they subtend equal angles at the centre.
items.answer: Let AB and CD be equal chords of a circle with centre O. Consider triangles AOB and COD. In these, OA equals OC because both are radii, OB equals OD because both are radii, and AB equals CD by hypothesis. So the two triangles are congruent by the side-side-side criterion. Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal, so angle AOB equals angle COD. Hence equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. The converse also holds, by the same triangles and the side-angle-side criterion.

items.stem: Explain why the angle in a semicircle is always a right angle, using the central angle theorem.
items.answer: Let AB be a diameter of a circle with centre O, and let P be any other point on the circle. The arc AB not containing P is a semicircle, and the angle it subtends at the centre is the straight angle AOB, which is 180 degrees. By the central angle theorem, the angle the same arc subtends at any point on the remaining circumference is half the angle at the centre. So angle APB equals half of 180 degrees, that is 90 degrees. Since P was any point on the circle other than A or B, the angle is a right angle wherever P is placed, which is why the result is stated for the whole semicircle.

items.stem: Prove that angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
items.answer: Let AB be a chord of a circle with centre O, and let P and Q be two points on the same side of AB, that is in the same segment. Consider the arc AB on the other side of the chord. By the central angle theorem, the angle this arc subtends at the centre, angle AOB, is twice the angle it subtends at P, and by the same theorem it is also twice the angle it subtends at Q. So angle APB equals half of angle AOB and angle AQB equals half of angle AOB. Two quantities equal to the same quantity are equal to each other, so angle APB equals angle AQB. Hence angles in the same segment are equal. This also explains why they are unequal in opposite segments: there the two angles are halves of the two different arcs, which add to 360 degrees, so the angles add to 180 degrees instead.

items.stem: Where does the circumcentre of a right-angled triangle lie, and why?
items.answer: It lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse. The reason follows from the angle in a semicircle. If the triangle has a right angle at C, then consider the circle with the hypotenuse AB as diameter; every point on that circle sees AB at a right angle, so C lies on it. That circle therefore passes through all three vertices and is the circumcircle, and its centre is the midpoint of AB. A useful consequence is that in a right-angled triangle the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices, at a distance of half the hypotenuse. For an acute triangle the circumcentre is inside, and for an obtuse triangle it is outside, so the right-angled case is exactly the boundary where it lands on a side.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees. Reason (R): A diameter subtends a straight angle at the centre. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and halving the straight angle of 180 degrees at the centre is exactly what gives the right angle at the circumference.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Halving the central straight angle is precisely the reason.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A diameter does subtend 180 degrees at the centre.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: The angle in a semicircle is genuinely a right angle.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Exactly one circle passes through any two points. Reason (R): The centre must lie on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: every point of the perpendicular bisector serves as a centre, so infinitely many circles pass through two points.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: The bisector has infinitely many points, each giving a different circle.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The centre genuinely must lie on the perpendicular bisector.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Three non-collinear points fix a unique circle, but two do not.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Every rectangle is cyclic. Reason (R): Opposite angles of a rectangle add to 180 degrees. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and supplementary opposite angles are exactly the condition for a quadrilateral to be cyclic.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Supplementary opposite angles is precisely the cyclic condition.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Each angle is 90 degrees, so opposite angles add to 180.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: A circle through the four corners of a rectangle always exists.

items.concept: Equal Chords are Equidistant from Centre
items.stem: Assertion (A): A chord nearer the centre is longer. Reason (R): The distance from the centre, half the chord and the radius form a right-angled triangle. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and in that right-angled triangle the radius is fixed, so a smaller distance forces a larger half-chord.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: The fixed hypotenuse is exactly why the two legs trade off.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The perpendicular from the centre does create such a triangle.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: The diameter, at distance zero, is the longest chord of all.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
items.explanation: A chord through the centre is the longest possible, and that chord is the diameter.

options.why: Chords get longer as they approach the centre, and the diameter passes through it.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the radius is a chord of the circle.
items.explanation: A chord joins two points on the circle, but a radius joins the centre to one point on it.

options.why: One end of a radius is the centre, which does not lie on the circle.

items.concept: Angle Subtended by an Arc at Centre
items.stem: State whether true or false: an arc subtends twice the angle at the centre as at the circumference.
items.explanation: The central angle theorem states exactly this relation for the same arc.

options.why: The central angle is twice the angle at the remaining circumference.

items.stem: State whether true or false: every rhombus is a cyclic quadrilateral.
items.explanation: A cyclic parallelogram must be a rectangle, so only a rhombus that is also a square is cyclic.

options.why: Equal opposite angles must also be supplementary, forcing right angles, so only a square qualifies.

items.stem: A chord passing through the centre of a circle is called a ___________.
items.answer: diameter

items.stem: The angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is ___________ degrees.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to ___________ degrees.
The point equidistant from all three vertices of a triangle is its ___________.
items.answer: circumcentre

items.stem: State and explain the chord properties of a circle that relate to the perpendicular from the centre.
items.answer: The first property is that the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. The reason is that joining the centre to the two ends of the chord gives two right-angled triangles sharing the perpendicular as one leg and having equal hypotenuses, since both are radii; the triangles are congruent, so the two halves of the chord are equal. The second property is the converse: the line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to that chord, proved by the same pair of congruent triangles read the other way. The third related property is that equal chords are equidistant from the centre, and conversely chords equidistant from the centre are equal. Together these let a chord length and its distance from the centre be computed from each other using the Pythagoras theorem, since the radius, the distance and half the chord always form a right-angled triangle with the radius as hypotenuse.

items.concept: Angle Subtended by an Arc at Centre
items.stem: In a circle with centre O, an arc AB subtends 110 degrees at the centre. Find the angle it subtends at a point P on the major arc, and the angle at a point Q on the minor arc, explaining the difference.
items.answer: The angle at a point on the major arc is half the central angle, so angle APB equals half of 110 degrees, which is 55 degrees. For the point Q on the minor arc, the relevant arc is the other one, AB going the long way round, and that arc subtends 360 minus 110, which is 250 degrees at the centre. So angle AQB equals half of 250 degrees, which is 125 degrees. The difference arises because P and Q lie in opposite segments and therefore see different arcs. Notice that 55 plus 125 equals 180 degrees, which is exactly the cyclic quadrilateral property: APBQ is a cyclic quadrilateral, and its opposite angles at P and Q are supplementary. This is a useful check on any answer of this kind.

items.concept: Unique Circle Through Three Non-collinear Points
items.stem: Explain why three non-collinear points determine exactly one circle, and why three collinear points determine none.
items.answer: Let the three points be A, B and C. A circle through A and B must have its centre equidistant from both, so the centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Likewise a circle through B and C must have its centre on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Any circle through all three must therefore have its centre on both bisectors, that is at their point of intersection. If A, B and C are not collinear then AB and BC are not parallel, so their perpendicular bisectors are not parallel either and meet at exactly one point O. Taking the radius as OA, which equals OB and OC, gives one circle through all three, and there can be no other because the centre was forced. If the three points are collinear then AB and BC lie along the same line, so their perpendicular bisectors are both perpendicular to that line and are therefore parallel and distinct. Parallel distinct lines never meet, so no point is equidistant from all three, and no circle passes through them. This is also why the circumcentre construction is the standard way to draw the circle through three given points.

items.stem: Prove that the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, and discuss what the converse allows you to do.
items.answer: Let ABCD be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle with centre O. Consider the diagonal AC, which divides the circle into two arcs. The arc ABC subtends some angle at the centre, call it x, and the arc ADC subtends the rest, 360 minus x. By the central angle theorem, the angle at D subtended by arc ABC is half of x, and the angle at B subtended by arc ADC is half of 360 minus x. Adding, angle B plus angle D equals half of x plus half of 360 minus x, which is half of 360, that is 180 degrees. The same argument with the diagonal BD shows angle A plus angle C equals 180 degrees. So both pairs of opposite angles are supplementary. The converse states that if one pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary then the quadrilateral is cyclic. This is valuable because it turns a statement about angles into a statement about four points lying on a circle, which is otherwise hard to establish. It is the standard tool for proving four points concyclic, and it immediately settles related questions: a parallelogram is cyclic only when it is a rectangle, since its equal opposite angles must also be supplementary and so must each be 90 degrees.

items.stem: A circle has radius 5 cm. Find the length of a chord that passes through the centre.
items.answer: A chord through the centre is a diameter, and the diameter is twice the radius. So its length is 2 times 5 cm, which is 10 cm. This is also the longest chord the circle has.

items.stem: A chord of length 24 cm is drawn in a circle of radius 13 cm. Find its distance from the centre.
items.answer: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so half the chord is 12 cm. This gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 13 cm, one leg 12 cm and the distance d as the other leg. By the Pythagoras theorem, 13 squared equals 12 squared plus d squared, so 169 = 144 + d squared, giving d squared = 25 and d = 5 cm.

items.stem: Two parallel chords of a circle of radius 10 cm have lengths 16 cm and 12 cm. Find the distance between them, considering both possible arrangements.
items.answer: For the 16 cm chord, half is 8 cm, so its distance from the centre is the square root of (100 - 64), which is 6 cm. For the 12 cm chord, half is 6 cm, so its distance is the square root of (100 - 36), which is 8 cm. Two cases arise. If the chords are on the same side of the centre, the distance between them is 8 minus 6, which is 2 cm. If they are on opposite sides, the distance is 8 plus 6, which is 14 cm. Both answers are valid, and the question has two solutions because the chord lengths fix the distances from the centre but not which side of it each chord lies on. Stating both is part of a complete answer.

items.stem: Match each term in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: (a) radius, (b) chord, (c) diameter, (d) arc. Column II: (i) a part of the circle itself, (ii) a chord through the centre, (iii) centre to a point on the circle, (iv) joins two points on the circle.
items.answer: (a) radius - (iii) centre to a point on the circle. (b) chord - (iv) joins two points on the circle. (c) diameter - (ii) a chord through the centre. (d) arc - (i) a part of the circle itself.

items.stem: Match each centre in Column I with the lines that determine it in Column II. Column I: (a) circumcentre, (b) incentre, (c) centroid, (d) orthocentre. Column II: (i) medians, (ii) altitudes, (iii) perpendicular bisectors of sides, (iv) angle bisectors.
items.answer: (a) circumcentre - (iii) perpendicular bisectors of the sides. (b) incentre - (iv) angle bisectors. (c) centroid - (i) medians. (d) orthocentre - (ii) altitudes.

items.concept: Unique Circle Through Three Non-collinear Points
items.stem: Describe and draw the construction of the circle passing through three given non-collinear points.
items.answer: Mark the three given points A, B and C. With a compass, construct the perpendicular bisector of AB: set the compass to more than half of AB, draw arcs above and below the segment from A and then from B, and join the two intersection points. Repeat the same construction on BC to get its perpendicular bisector. Label the point where the two bisectors cross as O. Label on the diagram that O is equidistant from A, B and C, since it lies on both bisectors. Now set the compass to the length OA and draw a full circle centred at O. Check that it passes through B and C as well. Annotate the diagram to record that only one such point O exists, because two non-parallel lines meet exactly once, which is why exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points. Adding the third perpendicular bisector, of CA, gives a useful check: it should pass through O too.

items.stem: Draw a diagram demonstrating that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle for three different positions of the vertex, and annotate what stays the same.
items.answer: Draw a circle with centre O and draw a diameter AB through O, labelling both ends and marking O at the midpoint. Choose three distinct points P, Q and R on the same semicircular arc above AB, well spread apart. Join each to A and to B, so that three triangles APB, AQB and ARB are formed on the common base AB. Mark a right angle symbol at P, at Q and at R. Annotate the diagram with the measured angles to confirm all three are 90 degrees. Now add the radii OP, OQ and OR and note on the diagram that each creates two isosceles triangles, since OA, OB and the radius to the vertex are all equal; this is the reason behind the result. Label clearly what stays the same across the three positions: the base AB is the same diameter, the central angle AOB is 180 degrees in every case, and so each angle at the circumference is half of it. Label what changes: the shape and size of the triangle, and the lengths AP and PB. The point of the annotation is that the right angle does not depend on where the vertex is placed, only on AB being a diameter.

items.stem: Prove that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
items.answer: Let AB be a chord of a circle with centre O, and let OM be the perpendicular from O to AB, meeting AB at M. We must show that AM equals MB. Join OA and OB. Now consider the triangles OMA and OMB. First, OA equals OB, because both are radii of the same circle. Second, OM is common to both triangles. Third, angle OMA equals angle OMB, because each is a right angle by the construction of the perpendicular. The two triangles are therefore right-angled triangles with equal hypotenuses OA and OB and a common side OM, so they are congruent by the right angle-hypotenuse-side criterion. Corresponding sides of congruent triangles are equal, so AM equals MB, which means M is the midpoint of AB and OM bisects the chord. The converse follows from the same two triangles: if instead we are given that AM equals MB, then triangles OMA and OMB are congruent by side-side-side, since OA equals OB and OM is common, so angles OMA and OMB are equal; being adjacent angles on the straight line AB they add to 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees and OM is perpendicular to AB.
